# On-behalf-of delegation for AI agents

On-behalf-of (OBO) delegation carries a user's authority between AI agents and tools in Consul Agentic Runtime Fabric. Each hop exchanges the user's token for a new token scoped to the next destination. Consul workload identity still controls which services can connect, and your identity provider remains the only issuer of user tokens.

@include '../../../global/partials/alerts/beta.mdx'

To set up delegation, refer to [Configure OAuth clients for AI agents and MCP servers](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/identity/configure-oauth-clients).

@include 'alerts/enterprise-alert.mdx'

## Introduction

Workload identity answers which service is connecting. Delegated user identity answers which user the service acts for, and what that user can do at the destination. An agent that calls a tool for a user needs both.

| Concern | Handled by | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workload identity and mesh connectivity | Consul and Envoy | Which workload connects, and whether mesh policy allows the connection |
| User tokens and token exchange | IBM Verify | The user's authority, issued under your identity policy |
| Outgoing exchange | The MCP Sidecar's OBO processor in the calling agent's pod | A token scoped to the next destination |
| Incoming verification | The identity processor at the destination | A verified token before destination policy uses its claims |

Workload certificates and OAuth credentials have separate lifecycles. Rotating one does not rotate the other, and a valid mesh connection does not make a user token valid.

## How OAuth clients work

Consul registers an OAuth client with IBM Verify for each participating service, using dynamic client registration. Each client authenticates with `private_key_jwt`, a signed client assertion, instead of a long-lived client secret in application configuration.

| Service role | OAuth client | Role in delegation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ai-agent` | Yes, with an exchange credential | Exchanges tokens for outgoing calls |
| `mcp-server` | Yes | Acts as an audience for callers |
| `inference-model` | No | Does not take part in delegation |

The audiences an agent can exchange for come from its explicit upstreams. Each upstream's registered client ID becomes an audience. You do not list audiences yourself.

## How it works

1. The user signs in with IBM Verify. The application sends the request, with the user's token, to the first agent.
1. When that agent calls the next service, its OBO processor resolves the destination from trusted routing information and maps it to that service's audience.
1. The processor exchanges the user's token with IBM Verify for a token scoped to that audience, using OAuth 2.0 token exchange as defined in RFC 8693.
1. The processor verifies the returned token and replaces any identity headers the caller sent with claims from the verified token. The request then travels over the permitted mesh connection.
1. The destination's identity processor verifies the token before destination policy uses its claims. Verification does not trigger another exchange.
1. If the destination calls another service, its own processor performs a new exchange for that next audience. A token for one destination is never reused at the next hop.

The [Delegate user identity](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/architecture#delegate-user-identity) sequence diagram on the architecture page shows each step.

## Policy and failures

Mesh policy, delegated-user policy, and tool policy are separate checks. Verified user claims are inputs to policy. They do not grant tool access on their own, and human approval does not replace token verification.

For a delegated call, the following failures stop the call from going forward under the user's authority:

- The request has no user context.
- The destination has no audience.
- IBM Verify rejects the exchange.
- The returned token fails verification.

The call is never downgraded to anonymous or workload-only access.

The processor can reuse a cached token only for the same user, audience, credential generation, and token lifetime. An expired or invalid cached token does not extend a user's access during an identity provider outage.

## Security

- OAuth signing keys are separate from Consul workload TLS keys.
- Public verification keys can be shared for validation. Private signing keys stay out of catalog metadata, application configuration, logs, and plaintext proxy configuration.
- Consul stores each client's registration record, including its private key, in the Consul key-value store. Restrict access to it. Refer to [Protect the registration records](/consul/docs/agentic-mesh/identity/configure-oauth-clients#protect-the-registration-records).

## Limitations

- IBM Verify is the only supported identity provider.
- Consul registers clients only for services in the `default` namespace and `default` partition.
- Audiences come only from explicit upstreams in the local datacenter. Wildcard upstreams, centrally configured upstreams, prepared queries, peered services, and services in other datacenters do not become audiences.
- Calls without user context are outside the OBO flow and need their own authorization policy.
- OBO delegation does not authenticate calls to managed model providers.
